work_or_witness: Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España (Florentine Codex), Ms. Mediceo Palatino 218–20 · Florentine Codex, bk. 1, fol. 34v, image metadata
original_script: Latin alphabet, sixteenth-century colonial Nahuatl orthography in the Florentine Codex transcription
definition: The Florentine Codex uses teotl for figures including Tezcatlipoca; its digital edition renders the category as 'deity' in associated metadata, but that English label does not exhaust the Nahuatl term.
cultural_caution: Do not translate teotl as an exact equivalent of 'god,' 'monster,' mana, or a fantasy race. This is a colonial witness term with contextual, historical, and living Nahua significance; no pan-Nahua pantheon roster follows from it.

citations.locator: Florentine Codex, bk. 1, fol. 34v, image metadata
supports: The edition tags teotl and identifies Tezcatlipoca as teotl/deity in this folio's context.

work_or_witness: Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España (Florentine Codex), Ms. Mediceo Palatino 218–20 · Florentine Codex, bk. 1, fol. 34v, image metadata; Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España (Florentine Codex), Ms. Mediceo Palatino 218–20 · Florentine Codex, bk. 2, fol. 135r
original_script: Latin alphabet, sixteenth-century colonial Nahuatl orthography in the Florentine Codex transcription
definition: In the Book 1 image metadata, ixiptlahtli appears with teotl; in Book 2's Sun-feast passage, ixiptla is the image set up at Quauhxicalli. The witnesses support a context-specific representational/embodiment relation, not one single English noun.
cultural_caution: Never flatten ixiptla into 'avatar,' costume, idol, sacrifice token, NPC skin, or possession mechanic. Particular persons, images, ritual contexts, and colonial translators require separate interpretation.

citations.locator: Florentine Codex, bk. 1, fol. 34v, image metadata
supports: The edition tags teotl and ixiptlahtli for the Tezcatlipoca image context.
The Nahuatl and English translation describe the Sun's ixiptla/image being set up at Quauhxicalli.

work_or_witness: Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España (Florentine Codex), Ms. Mediceo Palatino 218–20 · Florentine Codex, bk. 1, fol. 34r, Nahuatl transcription
original_script: Latin alphabet, sixteenth-century colonial Nahuatl orthography in the Florentine Codex transcription
definition: Book 1's Tezcatlipoca passage names mictlan, tlalticpac, and ilhuicac together; it witnesses a set of cosmological locatives in that description.
cultural_caution: This passage does not establish a fixed, universal number or arrangement of Nahua heavens. 'Heaven' is a translation convenience, not a mandate to map it to a monotheistic afterlife or fantasy plane.

citations.locator: Florentine Codex, bk. 1, fol. 34r, Nahuatl transcription
supports: The Tezcatlipoca description names mictlan, tlalticpac, and ilhuicac.

work_or_witness: Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España (Florentine Codex), Ms. Mediceo Palatino 218–20 · Florentine Codex, bk. 12, fol. 14v, Lockhart note 1 and Nahuatl-to-English translation
original_script: Latin alphabet, sixteenth-century colonial Nahuatl orthography in the Florentine Codex and Leyenda transcription
definition: Mictlan appears among destinations discussed with Moteuczoma in Florentine Codex Book 12; a note explicitly says it may be literally the land of the dead but also that the named places may be caves reputed to access supernatural realms.
cultural_caution: Do not equate Mictlan with hell, an infernal alignment, or a universal nine-level underworld. The Leyenda and Florentine passages are distinct colonial witnesses.

citations.locator: Florentine Codex, bk. 12, fol. 14v, Lockhart note 1 and Nahuatl-to-English translation
supports: Mictlan is named with Tonatiuh ichan, Tlalocan, and Cincalco; the editorial note cautions that the places may be realms or caves of access.

work_or_witness: Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España (Florentine Codex), Ms. Mediceo Palatino 218–20 · Florentine Codex, bk. 12, fol. 14v, Lockhart note 1 and Nahuatl-to-English translation
original_script: Latin alphabet, sixteenth-century colonial Nahuatl orthography in the Florentine Codex transcription
definition: Book 12 fol. 14v lists Tlalocan among routes claimed to be known for Moteuczoma's relief; the associated note calls it a verdant seat of the rain and earth god only as one possible literal reading.
cultural_caution: Not a generic paradise, elemental realm, or game biome. The cited note explicitly preserves uncertainty about whether the named places were caves reputed to access supernatural realms.

citations.locator: Florentine Codex, bk. 12, fol. 14v, Lockhart note 1 and Nahuatl-to-English translation
supports: Tlalocan is named among the possible destinations and the editorial note gives a qualified interpretation.

original_script: Latin alphabet, colonial Nahuatl orthography in Florentine Codex materials
definition: The Digital Florentine Codex labels tonalpohualli as a Nahua ritual calendar and presents the associated day-sign sequence on Book 4 fol. 82r.
cultural_caution: A calendrical-divinatory complex is not a zodiac, personality quiz, clockwork game cycle, or universally identical Mesoamerican calendar. The edition's label is retained as a witness-grounded orientation only.

citations.locator: Florentine Codex, bk. 4, fol. 82r, image metadata
supports: The edition labels tonalpohualli 'Nahua ritual calendar' and lists its day signs.

work_or_witness: Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España (Florentine Codex), Ms. Mediceo Palatino 218–20 · Florentine Codex, bk. 2, fol. 120r, heading and Nahuatl transcription; Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España (Florentine Codex), Ms. Mediceo Palatino 218–20 · Florentine Codex, bk. 2, fol. 135r
original_script: Latin alphabet, sixteenth-century colonial Nahuatl orthography in the Florentine Codex transcription
definition: Book 2 fol. 120r is headed Tlamanaliztli and describes the forms of laying offerings; Book 2 fol. 135r's English translation likewise renders tlamanaliztli in the Sun-feast sequence as laying offerings.
cultural_caution: Offerings are not a generic payment, sacrifice meter, or consumable system. This entry preserves ritual language without treating any practice as spectacle or stripping it from colonial conditions of record.

citations.locator: Florentine Codex, bk. 2, fol. 120r, heading and Nahuatl transcription
supports: The manuscript section is headed Tlamanaliztli and describes forms of making offerings.
The English translation renders tlamanaliztli as 'the laying of offerings' in the Sun-feast passage.

original_script: Latin alphabet, sixteenth-century colonial Nahuatl orthography in the Florentine Codex transcription

supports: The passage has the heading Tlenamaquiliztli and describes the fire utensil, embers, flowers, and copal.

work_or_witness: Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España (Florentine Codex), Ms. Mediceo Palatino 218–20 · Florentine Codex, bk. 2, fol. 135r, Nahuatl transcription and Anderson–Dibble translation
original_script: Latin alphabet, sixteenth-century colonial Nahuatl orthography in the Florentine Codex transcription
literal_gloss: one who dies in war (contextual reading)
definition: In Book 2 fol. 135r, yaomiqui occurs in the Sun-feast passage whose English translation says those who died in war went to the Sun's home; the same passage records fasting, bloodletting, offerings, and captive deaths.
cultural_caution: This does not license a glamorized 'sacred warfare' category or a blanket claim that warfare and sacrifice had one meaning. The passage must be read in its ritual, political, colonial, and human context.

citations.locator: Florentine Codex, bk. 2, fol. 135r, Nahuatl transcription and Anderson–Dibble translation
supports: The passage includes yaomiqui and translates the relevant statement as those who died in war going to the Sun's home.

work_or_witness: Leyenda de los Soles in Códice Chimalpopoca · Leyenda de los Soles, UNAM ed., pp. 119–122, especially p. 121
original_script: Latin alphabet, colonial Nahuatl transcription as represented by the UNAM edition
definition: The Leyenda calls naollin (Four Movement) the Sun of 'those of us who now live' and gives it as the sign when the Sun is set in motion. Earlier pages in the same edition narrate other named suns and their destructions.
cultural_caution: World-age accounts are not one fixed Aztec apocalypse calendar. This form and translation belong to a particular colonial Nahuatl witness and edition; do not treat it as a countdown, game-era template, or pan-Mesoamerican fact.

citations.locator: Leyenda de los Soles, UNAM ed., pp. 119–122, especially p. 121
supports: The edition gives prior Suns and names naollin/Four Movement as the current Sun's sign.

work_or_witness: Códice Boturini / Tira de la Peregrinación · INAH digital Boturini introduction, lines 31–39; Mexica (Aztec) Mythology and Ritual Traditions · INAH, 'El documento,' lines 23–35 and 56–78
original_script: Pictorial-semantic codex notation; the INAH contextual edition uses the Latin-alphabet spelling Aztlan
definition: INAH describes the Boturini as recording Mexica origins from departure from Aztlan to before the foundation of Mexico-Tenochtitlan, and describes Huitzilopochtli as guide/motivator of the migration in that account.
cultural_caution: Aztlan is a source- and community-sensitive place-identity/migration tradition, not an archaeological coordinate, fantasy homeland, or a license to essentialize Mexican, Mexica, or Nahua identity. The Boturini is colonial, pictorial, incomplete, and tied to oral performance.

supports: INAH describes a colonial account from departure from Aztlan toward Mexico-Tenochtitlan and identifies Huitzilopochtli as migration guide/motivator.
The Boturini is pictorial, colonial, incomplete, and its production/reading require contextual caution.

work_or_witness: Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España (Florentine Codex), Ms. Mediceo Palatino 218–20 · Florentine Codex, bk. 8, fol. 1r, heading and first chapter
original_script: Latin alphabet, sixteenth-century colonial Nahuatl orthography in the Florentine Codex transcription
definition: Florentine Codex Book 8 opens by describing rulers and noblemen and their elections/government; it names Acamapichtli as the first Mexico tlatoani and records tlatocayotl in the Nahuatl heading.
cultural_caution: Tlatoani is not a fantasy king class, a generic monarch, or proof of a timeless centralized 'Aztec' state. It is a historical-political office whose authority must be read in the witness's specific Mexica/Tenochtitlan and colonial context.

citations.locator: Florentine Codex, bk. 8, fol. 1r, heading and first chapter
supports: The Book 8 heading discusses tlatoque and tlatocayotl; the text names Acamapichtli as the first Mexico tlatoani.
